analysis.one_liner: Bans the sale, manufacture, and possession of newly acquired semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines, while grandfathering existing guns.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 193 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote since April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, make, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons — defined by specific features and by a long list of named models including AR-15 and AK-47 variants — and any ammunition magazine holding more than 15 rounds. Guns already legally owned would be grandfathered in, but their owners would have to store them securely and run a background check before any private sale or transfer. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and has received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, people exposed to gun violence would gain a federal prohibition on the manufacture, sale, and possession of newly acquired semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding more than 15 rounds, with the weapons most commonly used in mass shootings named explicitly in the bill [S2][S3]. Existing owners would keep grandfathered guns but would face a secure-storage requirement and a licensed-dealer background check for private sales or transfers [S2]. States could also use existing justice grant funds to pay people who surrender covered weapons under buy-back programs [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon or a magazine holding more than 15 rounds, with the covered weapons defined both by features (pistol grips, folding stocks, threaded barrels, barrel shrouds) and by an explicit list of named models including AR-15 and AK-47 variants.

Grandfathers weapons and magazines already lawfully owned rather than requiring surrender, while requiring secure storage so that prohibited people cannot access them, and a licensed-dealer background check before any private sale or transfer of a grandfathered weapon.

Exemts hunting-style and manually operated firearms, antiques, rimfire guns, and a long Appendix A list of specific hunting and sporting models, limiting the ban to weapons the bill treats as combat-style rather than ordinary sporting arms.

Requires date-of-manufacture markings on newly made covered weapons and serial numbers on newly made magazines, and directs the Attorney General to keep a public record of semiautomatic assault weapons used in crimes.
Lets state and local governments use existing Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds to compensate people who turn in covered weapons through buy-back programs.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers, importers, and gun dealers lose a large legal market: the bill criminalizes making, importing, selling, or transferring the covered semiautomatic weapons and any magazine holding more than 15 rounds, though existing owners may keep what they already lawfully own [S2][S3]. Buyers who want a covered weapon in the future cannot legally obtain one, and sellers of grandfathered guns must run a background check on private transfers [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and would-be buyers

drawbacks.text: The definitions reach very common firearms: the feature-based tests cover most semiautomatic pistols with threaded barrels or braces and rifles with pistol grips or detachable magazines, and the named-model list sweeps in hundreds of specific products, which critics argue reaches ordinary self-defense guns rather than only military-style weapons.

The grandfathering provision means millions of already-owned assault weapons and large-capacity magazines stay legal and can change hands through background-checked transfers, so any reduction in their circulation would be gradual rather than immediate.

The bill makes mere possession of a newly acquired covered weapon a federal crime for ordinary citizens who are not law enforcement, exposing otherwise law-abiding buyers to prosecution and forfeiture.

Enforcement would depend on the already-strained federal background check and dealer-inspection system, and opponents argue people determined to obtain banned weapons through illegal channels would not be stopped by a purchase ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters point to the role AR-15-style rifles and large-capacity magazines have played in mass shootings and argue a federal ban, like the 1994 law that expired in 2004, would reduce the deadliness of those attacks. The honest costs are real: the definitions cover a wide swath of firearms that millions of Americans own for self-defense and sport, manufacturers and dealers lose a major market, and the grandfathering clause means the supply of covered weapons already in circulation persists for decades. Whether the safety benefit justifies those costs is the core of the dispute, and the bill got no hearing where that argument could be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced in April 2025 and has sat there with no hearing or vote ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Lucy McBath introduced the bill on April 30, 2025, with 193 Democratic cosponsors signing on the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction and the public action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since then.
Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat; no Republican signed on.
Because the House has not acted, the bill's restrictions, grandfathering rules, and buy-back funding provisions exist only on paper and have had no effect on anyone.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, firearms manufacturers and sellers are better off: the market for covered rifles, pistols, shotguns, and large-capacity magazines continues uninterrupted, and the legal status quo for gun owners is unchanged. Supporters of a ban have gained nothing beyond the bill's introduction and referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and the current market

for.name: Rep. Lucy McBath
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 193 Democratic cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred has taken no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — since April 30, 2025.

against.name: Gun-rights lobby (NRA and similar groups)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the earlier 1994 federal assault weapons ban and its successors and campaigns against new bans; no such group appears in the congressional record on this bill.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controls the House floor calendar and has not scheduled any assault weapons ban for consideration; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 194 sponsors and cosponsors of the bill are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on, making support almost entirely one-party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the legal domestic market for the rifles, pistols, and shotguns it names — including AR-15 and AK-47 style rifles, among the best-selling firearms in the United States — and bans a broad category of parts and accessories. Manufacturers lose current and future sales of these models.

The ban covers any magazine, belt, drum, or feed device holding more than 15 rounds, ending future domestic manufacture and sale of high-capacity magazines and adding serial-number and date-marking requirements for any that are still made for exempt buyers.

Dealers could no longer sell covered weapons and could only handle grandfathered ones through regulated, background-checked transfers, shrinking the retail product line and paperwork-free sales channels.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with no committee action and no Republican cosponsors. With a Republican House majority unlikely to schedule an assault weapons ban for a hearing or a floor vote, the realistic path is that it stays in the House Judiciary Committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 without ever coming to a vote, as similar bills have in past Congresses.
